Instead she took his face between her hands and said, “This time I go with you.”

“The protocol won’t change for personal reasons.”

Her thumb brushed the fresh bruise at his jaw. “I know.”

Simon closed his eyes. “You understand?”

“I understand.” She stepped back, letting the distance between them match the separation he had chosen. “And I’ll love you in the morning. If there is a morning.”

That was the problem. The drive contained a witness—a digital witness that had seen him compromise operational security and let one hostage die to save another.

“Protocol must survive me,” he said. “If not, there’s nothing.”

“Nothing would be better than watching you break.”

Simon turned away. Esther was wrong, and his duty was not to argue the point.

Later he stood in the bathroom doorway watching her peel off her dress, one careful hand against her side.

“You’re limping,” he said.

“I’m fine.”

Her hair spilled loose down her back. He resisted the urge to touch it and looked away.

“Lie down.”

“Not for a doctor.”

“A husband.”

“Then ask.”

He went to the bed and sat, his hands on the covers. Esther watched from the door, still half-dressed.

“Simon.”

“You’re going to ask me to break protocol again.”

She crossed to him slowly, stopping when the lamp’s light fell across her bruised side.

“Maybe,” she said. “Maybe not. But I’m going to ask you for something. Can you bear that?”

Simon nodded.

She sat on the bed opposite him and drew her knees up.

“I don’t want you to do this alone.”

“It was my mistake.”

“It was yours to fix. But if protocol means anything, you don’t have to watch the result alone. Not here.”

He reached for her. She flinched, then let her hand find his.

“This isn’t easy,” he said.

“Tell me something I don’t know.”

Simon smiled for the first time in days. “It’s a good story. About a man who broke protocol to save a woman’s life.”

“And a man who lost her because of it.”

“Two stories.”

“Which do you want to remember?”

He touched her hair, feeling the silk of it between his fingers. “Both.”

Esther leaned closer, pressing her side against him. “Good answer.”

“It’s going to hurt.”

“Yes.”

They kissed in the way married people do, without urgency and without expectation that it would change everything.

The dress fell to the floor. He watched the black cloth pool on the carpet, felt the warm weight of her body shift onto his.

“You’re tense,” she said.

“It’s a good story.”

Her laugh was brief but real. “Just because it’s true doesn’t mean you have to tell it.”

Simon let his hands find her waist, feeling the dip of the scar there.

“You’re right.”

“I usually am.”

He rolled her onto her back and brushed a lock of hair from her face.

“This side,” she said. “The left. Like last time.”

Simon kissed her shoulder where the bandage ended.

“Better,” she said, her voice small.

“I could be a doctor,” he said. “Maybe.”

“Probably not.”

She let her hands rest on his chest. Her fingers touched his sternum and traced the line of his ribs, counting him.

“You’re warm,” she said.

“It’s your doing.”

Simon watched her face change as his hand moved lower, the amusement giving way to something less certain. He pulled her nightdress up her thighs, kissing his way there.

Esther caught his hair when his mouth found her.

“Simon.”

“Yes.”

Her name came out as a breath. He lifted her legs and settled his mouth at her entrance. She caught his hair again when he moved inside her, and this time he let it happen, knowing the tug wouldn’t be an end to anything.

He tasted her wet heat, moving slowly because the slow part was all he had left.

Esther’s hand moved to his hair.

“Tell me,” she said. “The story.”

“Not now.”

“Then when?”

He lifted his head, meeting her eyes.

“Morning,” he said. “If we wake up.”

Her laughter was small and sure. “Simon, you are terrible.”

He smiled against her skin.

“Maybe,” he said. “But you’re married to me. So you can’t get out of it.”

She shifted her weight, bringing his head lower.

“And this part?” she asked. “Is this protocol too?”

“Maybe,” he said again.

Her breath caught under him. Simon pressed closer, letting the motion build between them.

“I’m not going to watch you break,” she said. “Not if you take me with you.”

His name was a sound she made, a rhythm she let him set. Simon touched her breast, felt her press closer.

“Remember?” he said. “The story.”

Esther opened her eyes. “Which part?”

Simon watched the light fall across her face, the way it made the planes of her cheekbone catch and fade.

“The part where you said yes.”

“I did say yes.”

“You still are.”

He pulled back, watching her face.

“Always,” she said.

Simon kissed her again, felt her hands on his shoulders.

“And protocol?” she asked.

“Protocol,” he agreed.

They went to bed, both of them bruised, both of them knowing better than to expect anything would be different tomorrow. But there was tomorrow, and that was something.

The drive rested on the bedside table. Simon watched Esther fall asleep.

“You remember?” he asked.

She smiled, her eyes closed.

“Yes,” she said. “The story.”

“Good,” he said. “Because it’s not over yet.”

“No.” She yawned, her eyelids fluttering open. “But tomorrow might be better.”

“Maybe,” he agreed.

Esther kissed him then, the soft press of her lips against his.

“Protocol?” she asked.

Simon smiled.

“Protocol,” he said. “And the story.”

She fell asleep.

The drive waited, its data intact, its seal broken. Simon turned off the light and watched the patterns her breath made against the dark.

He fell asleep too, knowing nothing had changed and everything might.
